lead: A resistor opposes current by a fixed amount. An inductor and a capacitor also oppose, but they delay or advance the current, so a single number cannot describe them. Impedance Z = V/I is the fix: a complex number whose magnitude is the size ratio and whose angle is the phase shift. Written as Z = R + jX, it combines in series and parallel exactly like resistance. Every AC design — a motor starter, a 50 Ω antenna feed, a filter on a power supply — is an impedance calculation. Admittance Y = 1/Z is the same fact upside down.
prereq: You need: phasors and the j operator from 3.2, plus complex number arithmetic.

blocks.text: In DC the ratio V/I is R. At one fixed frequency the ratio is still meaningful, because every voltage and current is a phasor. That ratio is the impedance.

Each element gives one impedance. A resistor does not shift phase, so Z<sub>R</sub> = R at 0°. An inductor's voltage leads its current by 90°, so Z<sub>L</sub> = jωL. A capacitor's current leads by 90°, so Z<sub>C</sub> = 1/(jωC) = −j/(ωC). All three are in ohms (Ω).
Z = R + jX,  |Z| = √(R² + X²),  θ = tan⁻¹(X/R)
blocks.where: Z is impedance in Ω; R is resistance in Ω; X is reactance in Ω; θ is the angle of Z in degrees, equal to the angle by which voltage leads current.

blocks.text: X is the part that stores and returns energy instead of burning it. Positive X is inductive and the current lags; negative X is capacitive and the current leads. Keep the j: 8 + j6 Ω is 10 Ω at 36.9°, not 14 Ω.
Series impedances add: Z = Z₁ + Z₂ + …, because the current is common. The voltages divide in proportion: V₁ = V × Z₁/(Z₁ + Z₂).
Parallel admittances add: Y = Y₁ + Y₂ + …, or Z = Z₁Z₂/(Z₁ + Z₂) for two branches. The current divides as I₁ = I × Z₂/(Z₁ + Z₂); the larger impedance takes the smaller current.

items: Write every element as R + jX at the source frequency ω = 2πf.
Combine series by adding, parallel by adding reciprocals.
To invert a + jb, multiply top and bottom by its conjugate a − jb: 1/(a + jb) = (a − jb)/(a² + b²). The denominator is now real.
Use rectangular form to add, polar form |Z|∠θ to multiply and divide.

blocks.text: Admittance is the reciprocal: Y = 1/Z = G + jB, in siemens (S); older texts say mho. G is conductance, B is susceptance. Y<sub>R</sub> = 1/R, Y<sub>L</sub> = −j/(ωL), Y<sub>C</sub> = jωC. Series work is easier in Z, parallel work in Y.

Frequency changes the picture. |Z<sub>L</sub>| = ωL grows with ω, so an inductor blocks high frequencies. |Z<sub>C</sub>| = 1/(ωC) shrinks, so a capacitor passes them. At ω → 0 the capacitor is an open circuit and the inductor a short; at high ω the roles swap. This is the mechanism behind every filter.

examples.question: A coil of resistance 8 Ω and inductance 0.02 H is in series with a 100 µF capacitor across a 230 V, 50 Hz supply. Find the total impedance, the current, and the voltage across the coil.
steps: θ = tan⁻¹(−25.55/8) = −72.6°, so the current leads the supply voltage by 72.6°.
Coil alone: Z<sub>coil</sub> = 8 + j6.28 Ω, |Z<sub>coil</sub>| = √(64 + 39.4) = 10.17 Ω.
examples.answer: Z = 8 − j25.55 Ω (26.77 Ω at −72.6°), I = 8.59 A leading, and V<sub>coil</sub> = 87.4 V.
examples.check:
import math
R, L, C, V, f = 8.0, 0.02, 100e-6, 230.0, 50.0
w = 2*math.pi*f
XL = w*L
XC = 1/(w*C)
X = XL - XC
Zm = math.hypot(R, X)
th = math.degrees(math.atan2(X, R))
I = V/Zm
Zcoil = math.hypot(R, XL)
Vc = I*Zcoil
print(round(w, 2))
print(round(XL, 2))
print(round(XC, 2))
print(round(X, 2))
print(round(Zm, 2))
print(round(th, 1))
print(round(I, 2))
print(round(Zcoil, 2))
print(round(Vc, 1))

examples.question: The same coil (8 Ω, 0.02 H) and the same 100 µF capacitor are now connected in parallel across the 230 V, 50 Hz supply. Find the admittance, the equivalent impedance and the supply current.
steps: Coil branch: Z<sub>1</sub> = 8 + j6.28 Ω, |Z<sub>1</sub>|² = 64 + 39.48 = 103.48 Ω².
Capacitor branch: Y<sub>2</sub> = jωC = j314.16 × 100 × 10⁻⁶ = j0.0314 S.
Parallel admittances add: Y = Y<sub>1</sub> + Y<sub>2</sub> = 0.0773 − j0.0293 S. |Y| = √(0.0773² + 0.0293²) = 0.0827 S at −20.8°.
Z = 1/Y = 12.10 Ω at +20.8°, that is 11.31 + j4.29 Ω: the parallel pair is now slightly inductive.
I = V × |Y| = 230 × 0.0827 = 19.0 A, lagging the supply by 20.8°. The branch currents are 230/10.17 = 22.6 A in the coil and 230 × 0.0314 = 7.2 A in the capacitor.
examples.answer: Y = 0.0773 − j0.0293 S, Z = 12.10∠20.8° Ω, I = 19.0 A lagging. The same three parts in series were capacitive and drew 8.59 A; in parallel the coil current (22.6 A) is larger than the supply current, because the capacitor current cancels part of it.

traps: Sign of reactance: X<sub>L</sub> is +ωL, but X<sub>C</sub> enters as −1/(ωC). A capacitive branch has negative X, so the angle of Z is negative and the current leads.
Adding R and X as plain numbers: 8 + j6 Ω is 10 Ω at 36.9°, not 14 Ω.

Forgetting the quadrant. For a passive impedance R ≥ 0, so tan⁻¹(X/R) already gives the right angle (−72.6° in the worked example). The trap is the angle of a current or voltage with a negative real part: −3 − j4 and 3 + j4 both give tan⁻¹(4/3) = 53.1° on a calculator, but −3 − j4 lies at −126.9°. Check the signs of both parts and add or subtract 180° when the real part is negative.
Writing 'impedance of a capacitor is 1/ωC'. That is only the magnitude; the −j carries the −90° phase.
Unit slip: admittance is in siemens, not ohms. Y = 0.06 − j0.08 S has magnitude 0.1 S, which matches Z of magnitude 10 Ω.

quiz.q: Define impedance and give its unit.
quiz.a: Z = V/I for phasors at one fixed frequency; a complex number in ohms.

quiz.q: Write the impedance of an inductor and of a capacitor at angular frequency ω.
Why is |Z<sub>L</sub>| large at high frequency while |Z<sub>C</sub>| is small?
quiz.a: Z<sub>L</sub> = jωL grows with ω because a faster current change gives a bigger back-emf. Z<sub>C</sub> = −j/(ωC) falls as 1/ω because the stored charge per volt is fixed, so faster charging needs more current.

quiz.q: Z = 6 + j8 Ω. Find |Z|, θ and Y.
Z₁ = 3 + j4 Ω and Z₂ = 3 − j4 Ω are in series across 10 V RMS. Find Z, I and the voltage across each.
quiz.a: Z = 6 Ω at 0°; I = 10/6 = 1.667 A; |Z₁| = |Z₂| = 5 Ω, so each voltage is 1.667 × 5 = 8.33 V. The two phasors at ±53.1° add to 10 V.

quiz.q: A series RC circuit is fed at increasing frequency. What happens to the angle of Z?
quiz.a: Z = R − j/(ωC), so θ = −tan⁻¹(1/(ωRC)). As ω rises the angle shrinks toward 0°: the reactance falls and the circuit looks more resistive.

quiz.q: A 4 Ω resistor is in parallel with a −j4 Ω capacitor. Find the total impedance.

beyond: Not for the exam. Impedance is what a circuit simulator actually solves: SPICE builds a complex matrix from element impedances at each frequency. PCB designers fix trace impedance, often 50 Ω, so fast edges are not reflected. Power engineers use per-unit impedance for fault currents, and RF engineers read impedance and admittance on the same Smith chart. Next, impedance becomes a function of s = jω in Laplace transform analysis, and a whole two-port block is described by its driving-point and transfer immittances in two-port networks. Search: 'driving point impedance', 'impedance matching', 'self and transfer impedance'.
